place.en: the Mediterranean and the Near East
place.pt: the Mediterranean and the Near East

notYet: Not yet part of the Mediterranean and the Near East

stages.name: Cuneiform & hieroglyphs
stages.desc: Older scripts (cuneiform, hieroglyphs, syllabaries) or no writing; no alphabet yet

stages.name: Phoenician script
stages.desc: The 22-letter consonant alphabet of Byblos, Tyre and Sidon

stages.name: Greek alphabet
stages.desc: Phoenician letters adapted by the Greeks, with vowels added

stages.name: Old Italic & Etruscan
stages.desc: Alphabets of Italy borrowed from the Greeks: Etruscan, then Latin

stages.name: Aramaic
stages.desc: The Aramaeans' alphabet, which became the script of the Assyrian chancelleries

states.name: Cyprus
timeline: Greek settlers write their language in the Cypriot syllabary
Phoenicians from Tyre settle at Kition and write in their own alphabet

states.name: Lebanon
timeline: Byblos, Tyre and Sidon write a linear alphabet of 22 consonants
Ahiram's sarcophagus at Byblos carries the first full Phoenician text
Hiram I makes Tyre the leading Phoenician city

states.name: Syria
timeline: Luwian hieroglyphs in the Neo-Hittite cities; Aramaean tribes move in from the desert
The Tell Fekheriye statue: the earliest long text in the Aramaic script
Assyria takes Damascus; Aramaean kingdoms become Assyrian provinces

states.name: Turkey
timeline: Luwian hieroglyphs in the Neo-Hittite kingdoms of the south-east
King Kilamuwa of Sam'al carves his inscription in Phoenician letters
Ionian Greeks and Phrygians write alphabets of the Greek type

states.name: Tunisia
timeline: Libyan peoples of North Africa, without writing
Carthage is founded from Tyre (traditional date)

states.name: Greece
timeline: Linear B is forgotten: Greece has no writing at all
Euboeans at Lefkandi trade with Cyprus and the Levant
The earliest Greek alphabetic graffiti appear, with vowels added
The Dipylon jug at Athens: an alphabetic verse on a prize pot

states.name: Iraq
timeline: Assyrian and Babylonian scribes write cuneiform on clay
Ashurnasirpal II makes Kalhu (Nimrud) his capital
Under Tiglath-pileser III, Aramaic scribes work beside cuneiform scribes
Ashurbanipal gathers cuneiform tablets at Nineveh while the empire runs in Aramaic

states.name: Italy
timeline: Villages of the Italian Iron Age, without writing
The Nora stone: a Phoenician inscription in Sardinia
Euboean Greeks settle Pithekoussai and bring their alphabet
The Marsiliana tablet: the Etruscans adopt the Greek letters
The Latins of Rome and Praeneste begin writing with Etruscan-style letters

states.name: Egypt
timeline: Hieroglyphs and hieratic, under the priest-kings of Thebes and the pharaohs of Tanis
Shoshenq I sends a statue to Byblos; its king adds a Phoenician dedication
Greek traders settle at Naukratis; hieroglyphs and demotic remain the scripts of Egypt

events.title: Opheltas spit
events.text: A bronze spit at Palaepaphos carries a Greek name in the Cypriot syllabary, the first Greek writing on the island.

events.title: Aramaeans advance
events.text: Assyrian annals record Aramaean tribes pressing along the Euphrates, the people whose script would one day rule an empire.

events.title: Ahiram sarcophagus
events.text: Ittobaal of Byblos carves a curse on his father's stone coffin, the earliest full text in the Phoenician alphabet.

events.title: Hiram of Tyre
events.text: Hiram I enlarges Tyre and trades cedar, gold and craftsmen with the kingdom of Israel.

events.title: Lefkandi burial
events.text: A rich Euboean couple are buried with bronzes and jewellery from Cyprus and the Levant.

events.title: Yehimilk's temple
events.text: A king of Byblos records his restoration of the city's temples in Phoenician letters.

events.title: Shoshenq's statue
events.text: Abibaal of Byblos adds a Phoenician dedication to a statue sent by Pharaoh Shoshenq I.

events.title: Kalhu rebuilt
events.text: Ashurnasirpal II inaugurates his new capital at Nimrud with a banquet for nearly seventy thousand guests.

events.title: Tell Fekheriye statue
events.text: Hadad-yith'i of Guzana dedicates a statue inscribed in Assyrian cuneiform and in Aramaic letters.

events.title: Kition
events.text: Phoenicians from Tyre settle at Kition in Cyprus and rebuild its temple for Astarte.

events.title: Kilamuwa stele
events.text: The king of Sam'al boasts of his deeds in Phoenician, the prestige script of the region.

events.title: Carthage founded
events.text: By tradition, Elissa, a princess of Tyre, founds Qart-hadasht, the 'New City'.

events.title: Nora stone
events.text: A Phoenician inscription in Sardinia, the earliest in the western Mediterranean.

events.title: Al Mina
events.text: Greeks and Cypriots trade with Phoenicians and Aramaeans at a port on the mouth of the Orontes.

events.title: Kommos shrine
events.text: Phoenician sailors set up a shrine of three standing stones at a harbour in southern Crete.

events.title: Zakkur stele
events.text: The king of Hamath records a siege and his god's rescue in early Aramaic.

events.title: Osteria dell'Osa
events.text: Five letters scratched on a pot near Gabii may be the oldest Greek writing yet found.

events.title: Pithekoussai
events.text: Euboean Greeks settle on Ischia, the first Greek trading post in the west.

events.title: Gordion letters
events.text: Phrygians in Anatolia begin writing their language in an alphabet close to the Greek one.

events.title: Eretria graffiti
events.text: Potsherds from the Euboean city carry some of the earliest Greek letters.

events.title: Tiglath-pileser III
events.text: A new Assyrian king begins the conquests that bring Aramaic-speaking peoples into one empire.

events.title: Dipylon jug
events.text: An Athenian wine jug is scratched with a hexameter: a prize for the most graceful dancer.

events.title: Two kinds of scribe
events.text: Palace reliefs at Kalhu show scribes in pairs: one presses cuneiform into clay, one writes Aramaic in ink.

events.title: Damascus falls
events.text: Tiglath-pileser III takes Damascus and deports its people across the empire.

events.title: Bar-Rakib
events.text: The king of Sam'al switches from his local dialect to the Aramaic of the imperial court.

events.title: Cumae founded
events.text: Greeks from Pithekoussai found Cumae on the mainland, neighbours of the Etruscans and Latins.

events.title: Nestor's cup
events.text: A cup in a child's grave at Pithekoussai carries a playful verse in Euboean letters.

events.title: Motya
events.text: Phoenicians found an island town off western Sicily.

events.title: Carchemish annexed
events.text: Sargon II ends the last great Neo-Hittite kingdom, a home of Luwian hieroglyphs.

events.title: Karatepe bilingual
events.text: Azatiwada of Adana records his rule in Phoenician and Luwian hieroglyphs, side by side.

events.title: Marsiliana tablet
events.text: A small ivory writing tablet is inscribed with a 26-letter model alphabet in an Etruscan tomb.

events.title: Nineveh
events.text: Sennacherib makes Nineveh the capital of an empire administered in Aramaic.

events.title: Greek mercenaries
events.text: Psamtik I takes Ionian and Carian soldiers into his service at Sais.

events.title: Ashurbanipal's library
events.text: The king collects tens of thousands of cuneiform tablets, a library of the old script.

events.title: Formello abecedary
events.text: An Etruscan jar near Veii is inscribed with a model alphabet for learners.

events.title: Praeneste fibula
events.text: A gold brooch is inscribed in early Latin, though some scholars still doubt it is genuine.

events.title: Etruscan Rome
events.text: Under kings of Etruscan culture, Rome grows into a city that writes with Etruscan-style letters.

events.title: Naukratis
events.text: Greek traders found a port on the Nile delta, carrying their alphabet into Egypt.

events.title: Nineveh falls
events.text: Babylonians and Medes sack Nineveh; Aramaic outlives the Assyrian empire.

events.title: Adon's letter
events.text: A king of the southern Levant, probably of Ekron, begs Pharaoh for help against Babylon, in Aramaic on papyrus.

chartNote: Share of the area of nine present-day countries, by the newest script widely written in each. Regions are today's boundaries. Scripts overlapped for centuries (cuneiform in Iraq, the Cypriot syllabary in Cyprus, Phoenician in Anatolia), and the date when the Greeks adopted the alphabet is disputed between the 9th and 8th centuries BC; the map is a simplification. Large Egypt and Turkey weigh heavily in the shares.
